idiom_name: ES module per domain file, directory index as the published surface
implementation_notes: An ES module is one file: export marks the published surface, everything else is file-private (module scope) and import is the only dependency edge. A domain module is a directory whose index.js re-exports the intended names so consumers never import deep paths; in Node the package must be type: module or use the .mjs extension, and imports are static and hoisted. ESM bindings are live, so an exported object can be mutated by importers - the public state of a module is what you choose to export, not what you can protect.
pitfalls: Deep imports bypass the published surface: nothing prevents ./billing/ledger.js from being imported directly, so the boundary is convention plus code review (or the package.json exports field).
Barrels that re-export everything make internals public by accident, obscure where a name comes from, and invite cycles.

Cycles are allowed and only fail at run time: partially evaluated modules yield reference errors or half-initialised exports, so the dependency direction must be checked by tooling rather than by the loader.

variants.name: CommonJS (require / module.exports)
variants.idiom_name: CommonJS: a module.exports object per file, require for dependencies
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-ES2015 Node module system: a file is a module, its published surface is whatever is assigned to module.exports, and require() returns a fully evaluated, mutable export object. It remains the format of much of npm and differs where it matters for the pattern: exports can be patched from outside, there are no live bindings or temporal-dead-zone errors, and Node resolves extensionless paths and index.js automatically, which makes deep imports into another module's internals easy and invisible.
pitfalls: Export objects are mutable, so any consumer can patch another module's published surface at run time.
Extension resolution magic means renaming a file inside a module can silently change what ./billing resolves to.
ESM and CommonJS interop (default-export wrapping, importing CJS from ESM) makes a dual-published module look like two different modules.
